grammar.title: Future forms: will, going to and the present continuous
grammar.summary: Use going to for plans you have already decided and for predictions based on what you can see now. Use the present continuous for fixed arrangements with a time or place. Use will for decisions you make while speaking, offers, promises and predictions based on your opinion.
grammar.summaryMn: 'Going to' — өмнө нь шийдсэн төлөвлөгөө, одоо харагдаж буй зүйлд тулгуурласан таамаг. Present continuous — цаг, газар нь тохирсон тодорхой уулзалт, зохион байгуулалт. 'Will' — ярьж байхдаа гаргасан шийдвэр, санал болгох, амлах, өөрийн бодолд тулгуурласан таамаг.
structure: will / won't + base verb: I'll help you. It won't be easy.
am / is / are going to + base verb: I'm going to study law.
am / is / are + verb-ing + future time: I'm meeting my tutor on Friday.
Questions: Will you…? · Are you going to…? · What are you doing tomorrow?

usage.example: I'm going to take the IELTS exam next year.
usage.useMn: Өмнө нь шийдсэн төлөвлөгөө, санаа зорилго

usage.use: Fixed arrangements with a time or place
usage.example: I'm meeting my study group at six this evening.
usage.useMn: Цаг, газар нь тохирсон уулзалт, зохион байгуулалт

usage.use: Decisions made at the moment of speaking
usage.example: The library's closed? OK, I'll study at home.
Don't worry, I'll help you with your essay.

usage.use: Predictions: will (opinion) / going to (evidence you can see now)
usage.example: I think the exam will be hard. / Look at these questions — this is going to be difficult!
usage.useMn: Таамаг: will — өөрийн бодол; going to — одоо харагдаж буй баримт

contrast.with: will vs going to vs present continuous

pairs.a: Oh, the college is open now? I'll call them.

pairs.why: 'Will' = I decide now, while speaking. 'Going to' = I decided before.

pairs.a: I'm going to learn Spanish one day.
pairs.b: I'm starting a Spanish course on Monday.
pairs.why: 'Going to' = an intention, maybe no date yet. Present continuous = it's arranged and booked.
pairs.whyMn: 'Going to' — санаа зорилго, огноо тодорхойгүй байж болно. Present continuous — аль хэдийн тохирч, бүртгүүлсэн.

pairs.a: I think it will be a difficult exam.

pairs.why: 'Will' = my opinion. 'Going to' = I can see evidence now.
pairs.whyMn: 'Will' — миний бодол. 'Going to' — одоо харж буй баримтад тулгуурласан.

grammar.title: First conditional with if, when, as soon as and unless
grammar.summary: Use the first conditional for a real possibility in the future and its result: if + present simple, will + base verb. Use when or as soon as for things you are sure will happen, and unless to mean 'if … not'.
grammar.summaryMn: First conditional-ийг ирээдүйд бодитоор болж болох нөхцөл ба түүний үр дүнг хэлэхэд хэрэглэнэ: if + present simple, will + үйл үг. Болох нь тодорхой зүйлд 'when', 'as soon as' (…мөчид л), 'if … not' утгаар 'unless' хэрэглэнэ.
structure: If + present simple, will / won't + base verb: If I pass, I'll celebrate.
will + base verb + if + present simple: I'll celebrate if I pass. (no comma)
when / as soon as + present simple, will…: I'll call you as soon as I get my results.
unless = if … not: I won't pass unless I study. (= if I don't study)
The result can also be an imperative or can: If you feel nervous, take a deep breath.

usage.example: If it snows tomorrow, the school will close.

usage.use: when: something we are sure will happen
usage.example: When I finish university, I'll look for a job.

usage.use: as soon as: immediately after something happens
usage.example: I'll text you as soon as the exam finishes.
You won't understand the lecture unless you read the chapter first.
If you cheat, you'll fail the course.

pronunciation.title: Contractions: I'll, it'll, won't and gonna
pronunciation.explanation: In speech, 'will' is almost always contracted: I'll, you'll, it'll, we'll, they'll. 'Will not' becomes 'won't' /wəʊnt/ — be careful, because it sounds different from 'want' /wɒnt/. In fast, informal speech, 'going to' often sounds like 'gonna'. Using contractions makes you sound natural, and recognising them helps you understand fast speech.
pronunciation.explanationMn: Ярианд 'will' бараг үргэлж хураангуй хэлбэртэй байдаг: I'll, you'll, it'll, we'll, they'll. 'Will not' → 'won't' /wəʊnt/ — 'want' /wɒnt/-аас өөрөөр дуудагддаг тул анхаараарай. Хурдан, албан бус ярианд 'going to' ихэвчлэн 'gonna' гэж сонсогдоно. Хураангуй хэлбэр яриаг тань байгалийн болгож, хурдан яриаг ойлгоход тусална.

items.tip: Not 'I will' — just one quick sound: /aɪl/.
The t is very light: IT-l.
'We'll' has a long /iː/; 'will' has a short /ɪ/.

spokenForms.note: Informal speech only. Never write 'gonna' in an email, essay or exam.
The full form 'will not' sounds very strong or formal in speech.
Normal in speech and informal writing. In formal writing, use 'it will'.

questions.prompt: Studying something again before an exam is called…

vocabulary.definition: (British) to study again something you have learned, before an exam
examples: I need to revise for my history exam.
It's better to revise a little every day than all night before the exam.
vocabulary.note: In American English, 'review' or 'study for'. 'Revise' also means 'change and improve' a text: 'revise an essay'. The noun is 'revision'.

vocabulary.definition: to study a lot of information in a short time just before an exam
examples: I crammed all night and felt terrible in the morning.
If you cram, you'll probably forget everything a week later.
vocabulary.note: Informal. It usually has a slightly negative meaning.

vocabulary.definition: to learn something so well that you can remember it exactly
examples: I memorise ten new words every morning on the bus.
You don't need to memorise every date in the book.
vocabulary.note: British 'memorise', American 'memorize'.
vocabulary.mistake: 'Memorise' means learning something so you can repeat it. For 'keep in your mind' in general, use 'remember': 'I remember his name', not 'I memorise his name'.

vocabulary.definition: to write down the important information while you listen or read
examples: I always take notes during lectures.
She took notes on everything the teacher said.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'take notes' or 'make notes', not 'write notes' or 'do notes'.

vocabulary.definition: to give all your attention to one thing
examples: I can't concentrate with the TV on.
Try to concentrate on one task at a time.
vocabulary.mistake: Use 'on': 'concentrate on your work', not 'concentrate to your work'.

vocabulary.definition: not able to pay attention because you are thinking about or looking at something else
examples: I get distracted by my phone all the time.
He looked distracted during the lesson.
vocabulary.note: The thing that takes your attention is 'a distraction': 'My phone is a big distraction.'

vocabulary.definition: the process of getting better at something
examples: You're making good progress with your English.
I've studied for months, but I don't see much progress.
vocabulary.mistake: 'Progress' is uncountable: 'make a lot of progress', not 'make a progress' or 'progresses'.

vocabulary.definition: working well and giving the result you want
examples: Testing yourself is a very effective way to learn.
Cramming isn't effective in the long term.

vocabulary.definition: a special way of doing something
examples: This memory technique helps me learn new words.
Every student needs different study techniques.
vocabulary.mistake: Stress is on the second syllable: tek-NEEK, not TEK-nik.

vocabulary.definition: to give only the main ideas of something, in a short form
examples: Try to summarise each chapter in five sentences.
Can you summarise the main points of the lecture?
vocabulary.note: British 'summarise', American 'summarize'. The noun is 'a summary'.

vocabulary.definition: to find something very difficult and try hard to do it
examples: I struggle with English pronunciation.
Many students struggle to find time to study.

reading.title: Study Smarter, Not Harder
text: It's the night before an important exam. You've got a big cup of coffee, a pile of books and eight hours until the exam starts. Many students cram like this, but research shows that it isn't very effective. You might remember some facts the next morning, but you'll probably forget most of them a week later.

So what works better? First, spread your studying out. Instead of one long session, revise a little every day, and come back to the same topic after a few days, then again after a week. This technique is called 'spaced repetition', and it helps your brain move information into your long-term memory.

Second, test yourself. Reading your notes again and again feels useful, but it's quite passive. Close the book and try to write down everything you remember, or ask a friend to ask you questions. It's harder, but that's the point: when you struggle to remember something, you remember it better next time.

Third, take notes by hand, and don't just copy the teacher's words. Try to summarise the main ideas in your own words. You don't need to memorise everything — it's more important to understand how the ideas connect.

Finally, protect your attention. It's impossible to concentrate when your phone is buzzing every two minutes. Put it in another room, study for 25 minutes, then take a five-minute break. Many students are surprised how much less distracted they feel. Small changes like these won't make studying easy, but they will help you make real progress.

lessons.title: What are you going to study?

warmup.intro: What are your plans for this year? Have you already decided anything?

questions.prompt: I've decided! I ___ learn to drive this summer.

vocabulary.definition: to officially join a course, school or university
examples: I've decided to enrol in an evening English course.
More adults now enrol at university in their thirties and forties.
vocabulary.mistake: Use a preposition: 'enrol in/on a course', not 'enrol a course'.
vocabulary.note: British 'enrol' (enrolled, enrolling); American 'enroll'.

vocabulary.definition: the qualification you get when you finish a university course
examples: She has a degree in economics.
He's doing a master's degree in London.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'a degree in law', not 'a degree of law'.

vocabulary.definition: to finish your studies at a university successfully; a person who has done this
examples: I graduated from the National University of Mongolia in 2012.
Many graduates find it hard to get their first job.
vocabulary.note: The verb ends in /eɪt/; the noun ends in /ət/.

vocabulary.definition: money given to a student to pay for their studies, usually because they are very good
examples: She got a scholarship to study in Japan.
If I win a scholarship, I won't have to pay anything.

vocabulary.definition: the money you pay to study at a college or university
examples: Tuition fees have gone up again this year.
My parents helped me pay my tuition fees.
vocabulary.note: In British English 'tuition' can also mean teaching: 'private tuition'.

vocabulary.definition: one of the periods that the school or university year is divided into
examples: The autumn term starts in September.
We have exams at the end of every term.
vocabulary.note: Many universities, especially in the US, say 'semester' (two per year).

vocabulary.definition: a talk about a subject to a large group of students, especially at a university
examples: I've got a lecture on marketing at nine.
The lecture was so boring that half the students fell asleep.
vocabulary.mistake: Students 'listen to' or 'go to' a lecture — not 'listen a lecture'. The person who gives it is a 'lecturer'.

vocabulary.definition: to go to an event, a class or a place, especially regularly or officially
examples: You must attend at least 80% of the classes.
Over 200 students attended the talk.
vocabulary.mistake: No preposition after 'attend': 'attend a class', not 'attend to a class' or 'attend at a class'.
vocabulary.note: More formal than 'go to'.

vocabulary.definition: the buildings and land of a university or college
examples: First-year students usually live on campus.
There's a great café on the campus.

warmup.intro: Exams — do you love them or hate them?

questions.prompt: You are a student. Which sentence is correct in English?
questions.explanation: Students take (or sit) an exam. Teachers give or set exams.

vocabulary.definition: (British) to take an exam
examples: I'm sitting my final exams in June.
Thousands of students sat the entrance exam last week.
vocabulary.mistake: Students 'take' or 'sit' an exam — not 'give' an exam (Mongolian 'шалгалт өгөх'). Teachers 'give' or 'set' exams.
vocabulary.note: 'Sit an exam' is British; 'take an exam' is used everywhere.

vocabulary.definition: to take an exam again because you failed it; the exam you take again
examples: If I fail maths, I'll have to resit it in August.
The resit is on 20 July.
vocabulary.note: British English. American English uses 'retake'.

vocabulary.definition: a letter or number that shows how good a student's work is
examples: She got top grades in all her exams.
What grade do you need to get into medical school?
vocabulary.note: British English also says 'mark' (often a number: 85 marks out of 100). In the US, 'grade' also means a school year: 'She's in fifth grade.'

vocabulary.definition: to act in a dishonest way, for example by copying someone's answers in an exam
examples: He was caught cheating in the chemistry exam.
If you cheat, you won't really learn anything.
vocabulary.note: It's also a noun for the person: 'He's a cheat.'

vocabulary.definition: an exam you must pass to get into a school or university
examples: She passed the entrance exam for medical school.
The university entrance exam is in June.

vocabulary.definition: a practice exam that you take before the real one
examples: My mock exam results were terrible, so I'm studying much harder now.
We have mock exams in March.
vocabulary.note: British English. Often just 'mocks': 'How did your mocks go?'

vocabulary.definition: spoken, not written
examples: The exam has a written part and an oral part.
I'm more nervous about the oral exam than the written one.

vocabulary.definition: an official document that shows you have finished a course or passed an exam
examples: You'll get a certificate at the end of the course.
I need a certificate to show my English level.
vocabulary.mistake: Stress: cer-TIF-i-cate, and the end sounds like /kət/, not /keɪt/.

vocabulary.definition: making you feel worried and nervous
examples: Exam week is always stressful.
It was a stressful year for the whole family.
vocabulary.mistake: 'Stressful' describes the situation; 'stressed' describes how you feel: 'Exams are stressful. I'm stressed.'

vocabulary.definition: to be successful, for example in an exam
examples: I hope you do well in your exams!
She did well in the oral test, but not in the written one.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'do well', not 'do good' or 'make well'.

listening.title: Are you ready for next week?
listening.context: Emma and Jack are university students. Their final exams start next week.

lines.speaker: Jack
lines.text: Hey, Emma. You look tired. Are you OK?

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.text: Not really. I was up until two last night, revising for the statistics exam.

lines.speaker: Jack
lines.text: When are you sitting it?

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.text: Next Tuesday, at nine. And the oral exam for Spanish is on Thursday. It's going to be a really stressful week.

lines.speaker: Jack
lines.text: How did your mock exam go?

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.text: Badly. I got a D in statistics. If I fail again, I'll have to resit it in August, and I really don't want to do that.

lines.speaker: Jack
lines.text: You won't fail. You've been working really hard. Listen, I'm meeting a few people from our course in the library tomorrow. We're going to go through some old exam papers together. Why don't you come?

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.text: That's a great idea. What time are you meeting?

lines.speaker: Jack
lines.text: At two. And don't worry about the oral. You'll do well — your Spanish is much better than mine.

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.text: Thanks. I'm just worried I'll forget everything as soon as I walk into the room.

lines.speaker: Jack
lines.text: Everyone feels like that. But unless you sleep properly, you won't remember anything. So no more studying until two in the morning, OK?

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.text: OK, OK. I'll go to bed early tonight, I promise.

lines.speaker: Jack
lines.text: Good. And when we get our grades, let's celebrate.

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.text: Deal. See you in the library tomorrow at two.

speaking.sample: In my opinion, exams are useful, but they're not perfect. On the one hand, they make students revise, and they're fair, because everyone answers the same questions. On the other hand, exams are very stressful, and some people don't do well because they're nervous, not because they don't know the answers. For example, when I sat my university entrance exam, I was so nervous that I forgot a lot of things. I think teachers should use exams together with projects and oral presentations. If students do different kinds of tasks, teachers will get a better picture of what they really know.

vocabulary.definition: a teacher who teaches one student or a small group, or who helps a student personally
examples: I have an online tutor who helps me with my speaking.
Talk to your tutor if you're having problems with the course.

vocabulary.definition: a piece of work that a student is given to do
examples: I have to finish three assignments by Friday.
The assignment is a 2,000-word essay on climate change.
vocabulary.mistake: 'Homework' is uncountable, so don't say 'three homeworks' — but you can say 'three assignments'.

vocabulary.definition: to give a piece of work to a teacher
examples: Please hand in your essays by Friday.
I handed in my assignment two days late.
vocabulary.mistake: Students 'hand in' their work; teachers 'give' or 'set' it. Don't say 'I gave my homework' when you mean 'I handed in my homework'.
vocabulary.note: 'Submit' is more formal and is often used for online work.

vocabulary.definition: to not do as much work as you should, so that you are behind other people
examples: I was ill for two weeks and fell behind with my studies.
If you miss classes, you'll fall behind.
collocations: fall behind the rest of the class

vocabulary.definition: that you must do because of a rule
examples: English is a compulsory subject in most Mongolian schools.
Attendance at the first lecture is compulsory.
vocabulary.note: 'Optional' means you can choose: 'Music is optional, but maths is compulsory.'

vocabulary.definition: to leave a school, university or course before you finish it
examples: He dropped out of university after the first year.
Many people drop out of online courses because they lose interest.
vocabulary.note: The noun is 'a dropout' — a person who dropped out.

vocabulary.definition: to agree to join a course or activity by giving your name
examples: I've signed up for an online photography course.
If you sign up before 1 September, you'll get a 10% discount.
vocabulary.note: Less formal than 'enrol' or 'register'.

vocabulary.definition: the ability to make yourself do what you should do, even when you don't want to
vocabulary.mn: өөрийгөө хянах чадвар, бие даасан сахилга бат
examples: Studying online takes a lot of self-discipline.
I don't have the self-discipline to study at home every evening.

vocabulary.definition: extra time that you are allowed to finish something
examples: I asked my tutor for an extension because I was ill.
Can I have a one-week extension on my essay?

vocabulary.definition: to practise and improve a skill that you learned before but have partly forgotten
examples: I need to brush up on my French before the trip.
She's brushing up on her grammar for the exam.
vocabulary.note: Neutral to informal. British English also says 'brush up your English' without 'on'.

phrases.meaning: a clear way to start an email with a question
phrases.whenToUse: The first line of a formal or semi-formal email to a school, company or office. Too formal for a friend.
phrases.example: I'm writing to ask about your evening English courses.

phrases.meaning: a very polite way to ask a question or make a request
phrases.mn: …болох болов уу гэж бодож байсан юм
phrases.whenToUse: In polite emails and when speaking to people you don't know well. The past tense makes it softer, but it's about now.
phrases.example: I was wondering if I could pay the fees in two parts.

phrases.phrase: I'd be grateful if you could…
phrases.whenToUse: Near the end of a formal email or letter. Don't use it with friends — it sounds cold.
phrases.example: I'd be grateful if you could send me more information.

phrases.meaning: memorise something so you can say it exactly
phrases.whenToUse: In speech and writing, for poems, lists, phone numbers, etc.
phrases.example: We had to learn the whole poem by heart.

phrases.meaning: pass an exam very easily and with a very good result
phrases.whenToUse: In conversation or informal messages. Not in a formal email or essay.
phrases.example: Don't worry — you'll pass with flying colours!

phrases.whenToUse: Casual speech with friends, especially American English. Never in formal writing.
phrases.example: Exams start on Monday, so I really need to hit the books this weekend.

writing.prompt: You want to join an English course at a language school. Write an email to the school (100–140 words). Say what you are planning and why, mention one arrangement you already have that could be a problem, and ask two or three questions using if, when or unless.
writing.promptMn: Та хэлний сургуульд англи хэлний сургалтад суухыг хүсч байна. Сургууль руу имэйл бичээрэй (100–140 үг). Юу төлөвлөж байгаа, яагаад гэдгээ хэлж, асуудал үүсгэж болох аль хэдийн тохирсон нэг ажлаа дурдаад, if, when, unless ашиглан хоёр гурван асуулт асуугаарай.
points: Say why you are writing and what you are planning (going to)
Mention an arrangement you already have (present continuous)
Ask two or three questions (If I…, will I…? / When…, will…?)
phrases: I'd be grateful if you could…
I look forward to hearing from you.
writing.sample:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I'm writing to ask about your evening course in Business English. I'm starting a new job at an international company in October, so I need to brush up on my speaking and writing.

I have a few questions. I'm travelling to Japan for work from 3 to 10 September. If I miss the first week of classes, will I be able to catch up online, or will I fall behind? Also, will I get a certificate when I finish the course? Finally, I was wondering if I could pay the tuition fees in two parts.

I'd be grateful if you could send me more information. I'll sign up as soon as I hear from you.

I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours faithfully,
Bat-Erdene Dorj

reading.title: Never Too Late: Life as a Mature Student
text: Two years ago, Tsetseg Bat was working as an accountant in a bank. Today, at forty-one, she is in the second year of a degree in primary education. We asked her about life as a mature student.

Why did you decide to go back to university? — I always wanted to be a teacher, but my parents thought accounting was a safer job. When my own children started school, I helped them with their homework every evening and realised how much I enjoyed it. So I left my job and went back to university.

What's the hardest part? — Time. I have lectures in the morning, I study in the afternoon, and in the evening I'm a mum again. Some of the younger students stay up all night before a deadline, but I can't do that, so I plan every week very carefully. The technology was difficult at first, too. Everything is online now!

Do you get on with the younger students? — Yes, very well. At first I was worried they'd think I was strange, but now they often ask me for advice, and they help me with all the apps. We're a good team.

What are your plans? — I'm doing my teaching practice at a school near my home next spring. If everything goes well, I'll graduate in two years. I'm a bit nervous about the final exams, but I'm not going to give up now.

After that, I'm going to look for a job as a translator. I've already signed up for a short online course in business English, because I want to brush up on my writing. speaking.prompt: Compare studying in a classroom with studying online. What are the good and bad points of each? Which do you prefer, and why?
speaking.promptMn: Ангид суралцах болон онлайнаар суралцахыг харьцуулна уу. Тус бүрийн давуу болон сул тал юу вэ? Та алийг нь илүүд үздэг, яагаад?
speaking.sample: Studying in a classroom and studying online are both useful, but they're very different. In a classroom, you can ask the teacher questions straight away, and it's easier to concentrate because there are no distractions at home. You also meet other students. The problem is that you have to travel, and classes are at fixed times. Online courses, on the other hand, are flexible and often cheaper — you can study at midnight if you want. But you need a lot of self-discipline, and many people drop out. Personally, I prefer a mix. I'm taking an online course at the moment, but I also see a tutor once a week, so I don't fall behind.
